identity.title: ChaosBench: A Multi-Channel, Physics-Based Benchmark for Subseasonal-to-Seasonal Climate Prediction

problem.claim: Extend data-driven weather emulators to subseasonal-to-seasonal climate prediction for full Earth-system forecasting.

gap.claim: Existing benchmarks generally forecast only up to 15 days, lack broad operational baselines, and do not impose physics-based constraints for explainability.

contributions.claim: ChaosBench combines over 45 years of ocean, ice, land, and atmospheric reanalysis variables for Earth-system emulation with boundary conditions.
It adds physics-based metrics alongside deterministic and probabilistic metrics to assess physically consistent ensembles accounting for the butterfly effect.
It evaluates data-driven emulators against forecasts from four national weather agencies and reports strategies involving ensembles, error-propagation control, and physics-informed models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present ChaosBench as a challenging S2S benchmark integrating multi-component Earth-system data, physics-based metrics, and diverse agency forecast baselines.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that weather-scale methods fail on the S2S task, with performance collapsing to an unskilled climatology.

The authors report demonstrating several strategies intended to extend existing weather emulators' predictability range, including ensembles, robust error-propagation control, and physics-informed models.
The authors report that the benchmark, datasets, and instructions are publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: S2S climate prediction is presented as important for disaster preparedness and decision making, but harder than weather forecasting because of boundary interactions, the butterfly effect, and limited physical understanding.
Existing benchmarks are described as short-range, narrow in baseline coverage, and lacking physics-based explainability constraints.
ChaosBench extends the range to S2S, incorporates multi-component reanalysis over more than 45 years, adds physics-based metrics, and compares against agency forecasts and major data-driven models.
The authors report collapse of weather-scale methods to climatology, identify several extension strategies, and provide the benchmark materials online.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects expanded Earth-system variables to boundary conditions and physics-based metrics to physical consistency and the butterfly effect; it also includes forecasts from four national weather agencies, addressing the separately stated gap in operational baseline coverage.

lessons.interpretation: This makes the benchmark rationale traceable from task difficulty to evaluation design.
lessons.application: When introducing a benchmark, map each omitted capability to a specific failure mode and add a corresponding data, metric, or comparison component.
lessons.exception: This mapping may be unsuitable when the task's failure modes are not sufficiently established or cannot be operationalized.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative performance values, forecast horizons beyond the S2S label, dataset split details, or metric definitions.
The reported demonstrations and climatology collapse are not detailed enough to determine conditions, scope, or comparative effect sizes.

editorial_revisions.before: The abstract aligns each benchmark design choice with a named S2S difficulty: boundary-aware variables, physics-based metrics for nonlinear divergence, and operational forecast baselines.
editorial_revisions.after: The abstract connects expanded Earth-system variables to boundary conditions and physics-based metrics to physical consistency and the butterfly effect; it also includes forecasts from four national weather agencies, addressing the separately stated gap in operational baseline coverage.
